questions.stem: A brief on "the European EV charging market" covered only Germany and France. Logs show that the coordinator created two subtasks, "Germany EV charging" and "France EV charging". Both subagents returned thorough, well-cited findings, and the synthesis agent used all of them. What is the root cause?

options.text: The search subagent's web search tool ranks results by locale, so queries for other countries returned too few results to use.
options.why: No queries for other countries were ever issued. The subagents performed well within their assigned scope.

options.text: The coordinator decomposed the request too narrowly, so most of the requested scope was never assigned.
options.why: The subagents did their assigned scope correctly. The gap came from the decomposition.

options.text: The synthesis agent's context limit forced it to drop countries with less data, keeping only the two largest markets.
options.why: Synthesis used everything it received, and other countries were never researched.

options.text: The report agent's template has sections for at most two regions, so additional countries were truncated during formatting.
options.why: There is no evidence of this. The scope gap is visible earlier, in the subtask list.

questions.explanation: In hub-and-spoke systems, the coordinator owns decomposition. Coverage gaps that trace back to the assigned subtasks are decomposition failures.

questions.stem: The document-analysis subagent keeps producing generic summaries of the client's PDFs that ignore the specific research question. The coordinator invokes it with the Task prompt "Analyse the uploaded documents." Why does this happen?

options.text: Subagents don't see the coordinator's conversation, so the question, scope and prior findings must be passed in the Task prompt.
options.why: Subagent context is isolated, so anything it needs must be passed explicitly.

options.text: The subagent's `AgentDefinition` description is too vague, so the coordinator is selecting it for tasks it wasn't designed for.
options.why: Selection is working, since the right subagent is called. The problem is what it is told.

options.text: Subagents inherit the coordinator's context, but the system prompt overrides it. Removing the subagent's system prompt fixes this.
options.why: Subagents don't inherit the coordinator's conversation, and removing the system prompt would make things worse.

options.text: The PDFs exceed the subagent's context window, so it falls back to summarising only the first pages generically.
options.why: The summaries are generic regardless of document length. The symptom points to missing instructions.

questions.explanation: Subagents start with isolated context, so the coordinator must pass goals, constraints and relevant data in the delegation prompt.

questions.stem: The coordinator calls the search agent for five independent subtopics, one after another, and each brief takes about 9 minutes. Profiling shows that nearly all of that time is spent waiting on the sequential subagent calls. What is the smallest change that cuts latency?

options.text: Combine the five subtopics into a single, broader search request, so the search agent handles them in one invocation.
options.why: This loses focus and quality, and the work still runs serially inside one agent.

options.text: Move the subagent calls to the Message Batches API, which processes many requests concurrently at lower cost.
options.why: Batches have up to a 24-hour window and no latency SLA, so they're wrong for interactive latency.

options.text: Emit all five Task calls in a single coordinator response, so the independent subagents run in parallel.
options.why: Parallel spawning of independent subtasks is natively supported.

options.text: Lower each search subagent's `max_tokens` so each call returns sooner, reducing the total time across the five calls.
options.why: This risks truncated results and doesn't address the serial execution.

questions.explanation: Independent subagent tasks should be spawned in parallel by issuing several Task calls in one coordinator turn.

questions.stem: A developer defines four subagents with `AgentDefinition`, but the coordinator never delegates. It attempts the research itself with its own tools and produces shallow results. Which configuration issue is the most likely cause?

options.text: The subagent descriptions are too long, so the coordinator can't decide between them and falls back to doing the work itself.
options.why: Long descriptions might affect which subagent is chosen, but they wouldn't prevent all delegation.

options.text: Subagents must each be registered as separate MCP servers before the coordinator can discover and invoke them.
options.why: SDK subagents aren't MCP servers.

options.text: The coordinator's model is too small to orchestrate, and needs to be upgraded before it will delegate.
options.why: Model size isn't the configuration issue here. Delegation needs the tool to be allowed.

options.text: The coordinator's `allowedTools` doesn't include `Task`, so it has no way to spawn subagents.
options.why: Delegation requires the Task tool to be allowed.

questions.explanation: Subagents are invoked through the Task tool, so the coordinator's `allowedTools` must include it.

questions.stem: Briefs vary from narrow ("pricing of three SaaS tools") to broad ("state of climate fintech"). How should the coordinator's system prompt describe its job, to get the best delegation behaviour across this range?

options.text: Give a detailed 12-step procedure the coordinator follows for every brief, to ensure consistent and auditable output.
options.why: Rigid procedures break on varied requests and remove adaptive decomposition.

options.text: Give it the goal, quality criteria (coverage, citations, recency) and each subagent's purpose, and let it plan the work.
options.why: Coordinators work best with goals and criteria, not rigid procedures.

options.text: Give minimal instructions, so the model has full freedom to find creative decompositions for each request.
options.why: Without quality criteria, coverage and citations suffer.

options.text: Provide a lookup table mapping common request types to fixed subagent sequences, with a default for unknown requests.
options.why: This is brittle and can't anticipate the variety. It works like a procedure in disguise.

questions.explanation: Specify goals and quality criteria in coordinator prompts rather than step-by-step procedures.

questions.stem: To save time, a developer lets the synthesis agent call the search agent directly, and the report agent call the synthesis agent. Since then, debugging is difficult, some findings appear twice, and the coordinator's progress tracking is often wrong. What principle was violated?

options.text: Route all inter-agent communication through the coordinator, which tracks state, prevents duplication and aggregates.
options.why: Peer-to-peer calls bypass the coordinator's visibility and control.

options.text: Subagents should be stateless functions with no tools, so that only the coordinator can take external actions.
options.why: Subagents need tools to do their work.

options.text: Every agent should share one context, so any agent can see what the others have already found.
options.why: Context isolation is a feature. Sharing everything causes bloat and confusion.

options.text: Report generation should run in the same agent as synthesis, to avoid passing findings between two agents.
options.why: Merging roles doesn't address the uncontrolled peer-to-peer calls.

questions.explanation: The coordinator decomposes, delegates and aggregates. Routing through it keeps the system observable and avoids duplicate work.

questions.stem: A client asks: "What's happening in climate fintech?" Neither the client nor the team knows the relevant sub-areas in advance, and the landscape changes quarterly. Which decomposition strategy fits best?

options.text: A fixed chain (search, analyse, synthesise, report) with a standard set of subtopics reused for every climate brief.
options.why: Fixed chains suit known, stable structures, not open-ended discovery.

options.text: Ask the client to list the sub-areas, then run the standard pipeline, so the scope is agreed before any research starts.
options.why: Pushing discovery back to the client defeats the purpose of the research system.

options.text: A single agent with every tool and no decomposition, so it can follow leads freely without coordination overhead.
options.why: This loses parallelism and context isolation, and the context bloats on broad topics.

options.text: Adaptive decomposition: survey the landscape, prioritise the key sub-areas, delegate, and adjust as findings arrive.
options.why: Open-ended tasks need dynamic decomposition rather than a fixed chain.

questions.explanation: Use prompt chaining for predictable workflows and adaptive decomposition (map, prioritise, adapt) for open-ended ones.

questions.stem: The search agent runs four queries for a subtopic. Three succeed, and the fourth times out after 30 seconds. How should the search agent report back to the coordinator?

options.text: Return `status: error` for the whole subtask, so the coordinator knows to retry the full subtopic from scratch.
options.why: A generic status discards both the three successes and the diagnostic detail.

options.text: Return the three successful results as a complete success, since they likely contain most of the relevant information.
options.why: Silently suppressing the error causes undetected coverage gaps.

options.text: Return the three results plus structured error context for the fourth: failure type, query, partial data and alternatives.
options.why: Structured partial results let the coordinator decide how to recover.

options.text: Retry the failed query until it succeeds before returning anything, so the coordinator only ever receives complete results.
options.why: Unbounded retries hide the failure and can stall the workflow.

questions.explanation: Propagate errors with structured context and partial results. Avoid generic statuses, silent suppression and unbounded blocking.

questions.stem: Two credible sources give different figures for the same market in the same year: an industry association says $4.1B, and an analyst firm says $5.3B. What should the synthesis agent do?

options.text: Report the mean of the two figures ($4.7B), noting that it reconciles the available estimates from the sources.
options.why: That invents a number no source supports.

options.text: Prefer the analyst firm's figure, since commercial research is typically more rigorous than association estimates.
options.why: This is a blanket rule that resolves the conflict arbitrarily and hides it from the reader.

options.text: Report both figures with sources and dates, flag the discrepancy, and note any methodological differences.
options.why: Conflicts should be annotated with provenance, not resolved arbitrarily.

options.text: Omit the market-size figure and describe the market qualitatively, to avoid presenting uncertain numbers.
options.why: This throws away valuable cited information instead of qualifying it.

questions.explanation: Preserve claim–source mappings, annotate conflicting statistics with their sources, and separate established findings from contested ones.

questions.stem: Clients are finding statistics in final reports that can't be traced to any source. Investigation shows that citations are present in the subagents' outputs but get lost during synthesis. Which design change best fixes this?

options.text: Subagents return structured findings (claim, value, source URL, date), and synthesis carries the claim–source mappings through.
options.why: Provenance must be structured data that survives summarisation.

options.text: Add a citation step after reporting, in which the report agent searches the web to find a source for each statistic.
options.why: Retrofitting citations is unreliable and can attach the wrong sources.

options.text: Strengthen the synthesis prompt with a rule that every number must be followed by its source, plus an example.
options.why: This helps, but citations embedded in prose are still easily dropped during summarisation.

options.text: Remove the synthesis step and have the report agent assemble subagent outputs verbatim into sections.
options.why: This loses the cross-source analysis that clients pay for.

questions.explanation: Pass findings as structured data with metadata, so attribution is preserved across agent hops.

questions.stem: A client asked for a brief covering 10 competitors. The document-analysis agent couldn't open 2 of the uploaded annual reports because they were password-protected. Web search found little public information on those two companies. What should the final brief include?

options.text: A statement that the two competitors show no notable recent activity, based on the limited public information found.
options.why: An access failure is not evidence of absence. This misleads the client.

options.text: Coverage notes stating which competitors and sources were analysed, which couldn't be accessed, and why.
options.why: Explicit coverage gaps let readers judge completeness.

options.text: Nothing extra. The brief should present the eight analysed competitors cleanly, without drawing attention to the gaps.
options.why: Hiding gaps misleads the client.

options.text: A hold on delivery until the client provides unlocked versions, since a partial brief would breach the agreed scope.
options.why: A partial brief with annotations is usually more useful than blocking delivery.

questions.explanation: Annotate coverage in outputs, and never treat an access failure as "nothing found".

questions.stem: Meridian's clients increasingly question the reliability of briefs that mix fresh and outdated statistics, and established and speculative claims. Which TWO practices most improve trustworthiness? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Require a publication or collection date for every quantitative claim, so readers can judge how current it is.
options.why: Dates are essential provenance for statistics.

options.text: Separate well-established findings from contested or single-source claims in the structure of the report.
options.why: This signals uncertainty honestly.

options.text: Have the synthesis agent score its confidence in each claim and drop any claim it scores below 0.6.
options.why: Self-rated confidence is poorly calibrated, and dropping claims loses information silently.

options.text: Keep only sources published in the last 12 months, and discard older material to avoid outdated figures.
options.why: Recency alone doesn't make a source more credible, and this can remove authoritative baselines.

options.text: Have the report agent rewrite the brief in a neutral tone that avoids definitive statements about any finding.
options.why: Hedging everything equally hides the real differences in certainty.

questions.explanation: Provenance (sources and dates) and explicit uncertainty (established vs contested) are the core of trustworthy synthesis.

questions.stem: The synthesis agent needs frequent quick fact-checks, such as "confirm this company's HQ city". Each one round-trips through the coordinator to the search agent, adding about 35% latency. About 80% of the checks are simple lookups. What is the best change?

options.text: Give the synthesis agent the full web search and fetch toolset, so it can do its own research without delays.
options.why: This over-provisions the agent and blurs role boundaries.

options.text: Have synthesis collect all its fact-check needs and send them to the coordinator in one batch at the end.
options.why: This creates blocking dependencies and late rework.

options.text: Give synthesis a narrowly scoped `verify_fact` tool for simple lookups, and leave complex checks with the coordinator.
options.why: A limited cross-role tool cuts latency while preserving least privilege.

options.text: Pre-fetch and cache likely facts for every entity mentioned in the subagents' findings before synthesis begins.
options.why: Speculative caching wastes work, misses unexpected facts and can serve stale data.

questions.explanation: Scope tools to roles. Where frequent cross-role needs exist, add a narrowly scoped tool rather than full access.

questions.stem: The search agent has two tools: `analyze_content` (summarises fetched web pages) and `analyze_document` (parses PDFs the client uploaded). It frequently calls the wrong one, for example sending a web URL to the PDF parser. Which change most directly fixes this?

options.text: Rename and redescribe them with clear boundaries (`summarize_web_page(url)` vs `parse_uploaded_pdf(file_id)`, with when-not-to-use notes).
options.why: Overlapping names and descriptions cause misrouting, so make the boundaries explicit.

options.text: Add a system-prompt rule: "Use analyze_document only for uploaded files, and analyze_content only for web pages."
options.why: This patches around the ambiguity instead of fixing it at its source, in the tool definitions.

options.text: Merge them into a single `analyze(input)` tool that detects whether it was given a URL or a file ID.
options.why: Generic merged tools hide the distinction and are harder to describe and validate.

options.text: Validate inputs in both tools and return an error when the wrong input type is passed, so the agent can retry.
options.why: Useful as a guardrail, but it treats the symptom after a wasted call rather than preventing the misrouting.

questions.explanation: Tools with overlapping, generic names or descriptions get confused. Rename, split and describe their boundaries clearly.

questions.stem: The report agent has three tools: `fetch_template`, `render_chart` and `submit_report`. On its final step, it must always deliver the brief by calling `submit_report`, never as free text. Which `tool_choice` setting guarantees this on that step?

options.text: `{"type": "auto"}`, combined with a system-prompt instruction to finish by calling `submit_report`.
options.why: With `auto` the model may still answer in text.

options.text: `{"type": "any"}`, which requires the model to call one of its tools instead of replying with text.
options.why: This forces some tool, which could be `fetch_template` or `render_chart` rather than `submit_report`.

options.text: `{"type": "tool", "name": "submit_report"}`
options.why: A forced tool choice guarantees that this specific tool is called.

options.text: `{"type": "none"}`, with the report schema in the system prompt, and the JSON parsed from the final text.
options.why: This disables tool use and loses schema enforcement.

questions.explanation: `auto` lets the model decide, `any` requires some tool, and the forced form requires a named tool.

questions.stem: The firm has a catalog of 4,000 past briefs. Agents should be able to browse it and pull relevant briefs in as reference material. What is the most appropriate way to expose the catalog through MCP?

options.text: Generate one MCP tool per brief, named after its topic, so the agent can call the exact brief it needs.
options.why: Thousands of tools would destroy tool selection.

options.text: Add a summary of all 4,000 briefs to each agent's system prompt, so they know what exists without lookups.
options.why: This is huge context bloat on every call.

options.text: Expose the catalog as MCP resources the agents can discover and read, and keep tools for actions.
options.why: MCP resources are designed for content catalogs.

options.text: Mount the brief archive as a directory and let agents use Grep and Read to find relevant briefs by keyword.
options.why: This bypasses access control and structure, and it isn't available to remote agents.

questions.explanation: MCP distinguishes tools (actions) from resources (readable content), and resources suit catalogs.
